title: Somerset Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Somerset wells have a median depth of 80 ft, with a typical finished-well cost of $11,200-$20,000.
h1: Somerset Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Somerset means understanding mountain bedrock, not just looking at a nearby well permit. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 80 feet, but reported depths range from shallow wells to a deepest record of 720 feet. The same records show a median reported yield of 13.0 gallons per minute, although only 16 wells report a pump yield.

Most permitted wells are tied to unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. That makes neighboring well records useful for setting expectations, but not a guarantee for a particular lot. Access, drilling conditions, casing, grout, pump equipment, septic layout, and the intended household use all affect the final plan.

sections.heading: Somerset well depth depends on the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Somerset’s recorded well depth is shallow by mountain-well standards at the middle of the data: the median is 80 feet, and the middle half runs from 50 to 150 feet. Still, the range is wide. Fifty-eight percent of reported depths are under 100 feet, 33% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 7% from 300 to 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record is 720 feet.

That spread matters when comparing drilling bids. A bid based only on the median can be misleading if the lot sits over harder or less productive fractured granite or gneiss. Ask the driller how the price changes if the hole must go beyond the planned depth, and confirm what casing, grout, testing, and pump work are included.

sections.heading: Reported Somerset yields are strong, but the sample is small
sections.html:
The reported yield data is encouraging: the median is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 9.8 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-four percent of reporting wells produce 15 or more gallons per minute, and another 44% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Twelve percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, while none of the reporting wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

Do not treat those percentages as a guarantee. Only 16 wells report a pump yield, compared with 64 recorded as constructed. A well’s usable supply also depends on storage, pump sizing, and the home’s demand. An exempt household-use well has a 35 gpm pumping limit, but a buyer still needs to confirm the permit’s allowed use and conditions with Colorado DWR.

sections.heading: Somerset water levels are relatively shallow in the records
sections.html:
Eleven Somerset-area permits report a static water level. The median depth to water is 43 feet, and the middle half runs from 23 to 88 feet. That gives a useful starting point for estimating pumping lift and discussing casing and pump placement, but it is not a site-wide water-table measurement.

The available facts do not provide a water-level series by decade, so they do not establish a dropping or rising trend. Static levels can vary with season, nearby pumping, recharge, and the exact fractured-bedrock zone a well reaches. Before buying, ask for the original well construction and test records for nearby parcels and have a driller interpret them in relation to the lot’s elevation and geology.

sections.heading: Somerset permit history points to several local drilling records
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across the local history, with the largest period in the records during the 1990s: 65 permits. The records show 12 permits in the 1970s, 2 in the 1980s, 27 in the 2000s, 16 in the 2010s, and 18 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active named drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 22 wells; Wildcat Drilling & Pump, Inc. (Kissner, Billy D.), with 17; and Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.), with 13. Those counts describe permit records, not a current recommendation or proof that a company is available. Check licensing, insurance, references, and the scope of the written bid.

sections.heading: A Somerset well can cost more when drilling goes deep
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock such as granite or gneiss, the drilling model is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $5,200 to $8,000. A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $11,200 to $20,000.

That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. The deepest record reaches 720 feet, so an unsuccessful or extended hole can change the budget substantially. Get the contractor to separate drilling from casing, grout, pump, tank, trenching, electrical, water testing, and abandonment or dry-hole terms. Steep access and construction around an existing home can also affect the proposal.

sections.heading: Check mines, PFAS sites, septic space, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles of Somerset, the mapped environmental information includes 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 38 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. A map flag does not by itself prove that a parcel’s well water is contaminated, but it is a reason to investigate site history and test the water. Historic mining can also complicate access, ground conditions, and water-quality questions.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even when nearby wells perform well. Before building, confirm that the proposed well location leaves workable room for septic components, replacement areas, drive access, and the house foundation. The water right and permit must match the intended use; over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan for some uses.

sections.heading: Use nearby Somerset permits before you commit to a lot
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and surrounding wells, then compare depth, aquifer description, static water level, yield, and use. The local records are dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers: 166 wells are identified that way. Only 3 name the Mesa Verde aquifer, 1 names the Mesa Verde Group, and none are Denver Basin aquifer wells.

For a vacant lot, make the well location part of the site plan rather than treating it as an afterthought. Price access for a rig, confirm where drilling spoils can go, protect separation from septic work, and budget for a pump and storage system. If the property is near Paonia, Hotchkiss, Crawford, Marble, Lazear, or Redstone, use those areas only as broader context; the closest well records and the parcel’s own permit matter most.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Somerset, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Somerset is 80 feet, and the middle half of reported depths is 50 to 150 feet. Fifty-eight percent are under 100 feet, but the deepest record is 720 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce a wide range, so nearby permits are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Somerset, Colorado?
faq.a: The drilling model for Somerset’s fractured mountain bedrock is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the hole is estimated at $5,200 to $8,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $11,200 to $20,000. A deeper hole can raise the cost considerably.

faq.q: How much water do Somerset wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 16 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 9.8 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-four percent report 15 or more gallons per minute, while 12% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. The sample is limited, so no yield is guaranteed.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Somerset?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that every Somerset well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles are 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 38 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the specific well for ordinary drinking-water concerns and investigate local mining or PFAS history before relying on it.

faq.q: Are Somerset wells getting deeper or running lower?
faq.a: The available records show a median static water level of 43 feet, with the middle half from 23 to 88 feet, based on 11 reported measurements. They do not include a water-level-by-decade series, so they cannot show a reliable rising or falling trend. Ask for current testing and nearby construction records when evaluating a property.
